title: County of Anjou
capsule: The County of Anjou coalesced in the mid-ninth century when the Carolingian king appointed the Robertian Robert the Strong as count over the Loire valley territory, with Angers as its capital. The eleventh-century counts of the Fulk dynasty—particularly Fulk Nerra (r. 987–1040) and his successor Geoffrey Martel—built Anjou into the most aggressive territorial power in north-western France through a relentless campaign of castle-building and warfare against the counts of Blois. Geoffrey Plantagenet's inheritance of Normandy and his son Henry's accession to the English throne in 1154 folded Anjou into the Angevin Empire; Philip II of France seized the county in 1204, and it remained under the French crown until Louis IX granted it as an apanage to his brother Charles in 1246, who became king of Naples—the title was elevated to a duchy in 1360.
attestation: Boundaries from Seshat Cliopatria (Bennett et al., Scientific Data 2025; CC BY 4.0), digitized from standard historical atlases at ~0.07° resolution. Anjou's core boundaries around the Angers basin are well-established through medieval cartularies; contested frontier districts with Blois, Maine, and Touraine shifted frequently and are attested only at specific moments.
